A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CL-DiffPhyCon. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison, including matching renamed experiments and relocated proofs.

before.justification: v2 reports original simulations comparing control performance and inference time on Burgers’ equation and incompressible-fluid tasks, with additional visual results in the appendices.

after.justification: v3 retains the original empirical results and adds constrained and noisy control experiments, horizon sensitivity, boundary control, and double-pendulum simulations.

M1.justification: The two-model asynchronous controller, training losses, and Algorithm 1 are retained. The added pendulum implementation uses a Transformer and midpoint-ODE sampling, extending the architecture and sampler instantiations beyond v2’s U-Net DDPM/DDIM implementations. Appendix C primarily documents existing DDPM procedures rather than changing the original controller.

E1.justification: v3 adds Burgers’ control with actuator bounds, system noise, measurement noise, and sparse sensors/actuators; fluid boundary control; and a distinct double-pendulum task. The earlier FO and PO experiments remain as noise-free and half-domain settings, and the original fixed/random fluid maps are retained.

E2.justification: The original PDE comparator sets remain. The pendulum comparison adds DiffPhyCon-4, -8, -12, and -16 variants in Figure 7, extending the existing DiffPhyCon family. Its prose and Figure 8 instead name DiffPhyCon-15, leaving an inconsistency in one comparator label.

E3.justification: New protocols include full-domain scoring for sparse-observation/control experiments, 30,000 boundary-control training trajectories with 120-step DDIM sampling, and horizon comparisons at H=6, 10, and 15. Pendulum evaluation introduces PPO-generated training data, 290,000 training steps, 100 systems per evaluation, 200-step episodes, success rate, and function-evaluation efficiency. Main-table runtimes now average across settings rather than reporting each setting separately.

E4.justification: Beyond v2’s partial-observation and random-map tests, v3 adds explicit noise and actuator-restriction robustness tests. Appendix G.3 investigates horizon sensitivity, while Appendix H examines pendulum perturbation rates and supplies trajectory and phase-space case studies. These substantially expand diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: v2 reports averages and mentions repeated qualitative evaluations without specifying seeds or uncertainty estimates. v3’s pendulum experiment reports five differently seeded runs and mean results with ±1 standard deviation in Figure 7. This reporting improvement is confined to the added experiment; additional runs for the retained PDE results are not established.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial numerical and graphical results, including boundary-control objectives of 0.6169/0.7003 for fixed/random maps, horizon sensitivity, and pendulum performance-efficiency curves. Retained PDE objective scores are unchanged. The half-domain CL-DiffPhyCon runtime changes from 3.7516 seconds in v2 Table 1 to 9.7516 in v3 Table 4 without an explained setting change. Revised main-table runtime averages are not directly comparable to the earlier per-setting timings.

T1.justification: Equation 1 changes from deterministic action-sequence optimization to expected-objective optimization over a state-conditioned policy with explicitly stochastic dynamics. Proposition 2 receives a different brief proof argument. Theorem 1 and Proposition 1 and their proofs are retained; relocating Proposition 2 and spelling out DDPM specializations do not constitute new theoretical results.

C1.justification: The main contributions remain theoretically motivated asynchronous closed-loop diffusion control, reduced sampling cost, compatibility with DDIM, and strong physical-control performance. The expanded experiments support these existing claims without materially redefining their scope.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly acknowledges the absence of optimization-performance bounds under guided sampling, replacing v2’s future-work discussion of incorporating PDE priors. It also interprets short-horizon failure through inaccurate objective estimation, discusses memory tradeoffs, and explains sparse-control effects. Offline-training and broader-applicability limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix C adds explicit synchronous and asynchronous DDPM implementation formulas. New appendices document noise injection, actuator placement, boundary-control data and sampling settings, and pendulum simulation, training, and evaluation details. The anonymous code link in v2 is replaced by a named GitHub link. Conversely, v3 drops the previously disclosed half-domain RDM threshold pair.

R1.justification: v3 adds references covering MPC, Diffusion Policy, noisy dynamics, numerical integration, and double-pendulum control. The central positioning against DiffPhyCon, adaptive replanning, and sequential diffusion generation remains substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The problem setup and method explanations are extensively revised, with transition-model training presented before guided sampling and efficiency separated into Section 4.5. Proposition 2 moves to Appendix E, limitations move into the conclusion, and experimental appendices are reorganized. Terminology, the title, affiliations, and publication headers also change.

P2.justification: Tables 1–2 are substantially restructured around expanded scenarios and pooled timing columns. v3 adds sensor/actuator and fluid-domain diagrams, a horizon table, and pendulum schematic, Pareto, and trajectory plots. The earlier main-text Burgers’ comparison figure is removed, but its examples remain in the retained appendix visualizations; the fluid comparison figure is renumbered.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence for robustness and the performance-efficiency tradeoff through noisy feedback, restricted actuation, horizon sensitivity, and a distinct pendulum task with five-seed uncertainty. Expanded implementation information and explicit theoretical limitations also improve assessability. Incorrect noise-improvement percentages, inconsistent pendulum baseline labels, and the unexplained half-domain timing change weaken reporting, but do not outweigh these gains. The improvement comes from broader and more diagnostic evidence, not higher scores on retained settings.
